files.Purchase.lean:
/-
Purchase.lean — standalone Lean analysis model of the purchase rule.

This module models the same rule that `kernel.rs` implements
(`can_purchase (balance stock : u64) : Bool := balance >= 150 && stock > 0`).
It is an ordinary Lean analysis model only: it is not a refinement binding,
not a native contract, and it establishes no correspondence with the Rust code.

Rule: a purchase is eligible exactly when the balance is at least 150 and the
stock is positive.

Only the Lean core prelude is used. The proof is complete: no `sorry`, no
additional axioms, no `native_decide`.
-/

namespace Purchase

/-- A purchase is eligible when the balance is at least 150 and the stock is
positive. -/
def canPurchase (balance stock : Nat) : Prop :=
  150 ≤ balance ∧ 0 < stock

/-- `canPurchase` holds exactly when both defining conditions hold: the
balance is at least 150 and the stock is positive. The two natural inputs are
universally quantified. -/
theorem eligibility_exact : ∀ (balance stock : Nat),
    canPurchase balance stock ↔ (150 ≤ balance ∧ 0 < stock) := by
  intro balance stock
  constructor
  · intro h
    exact h
  · intro h
    exact h

end Purchase

In plain terms: applying the purchase-eligibility predicate to any balance/stock pair is equivalent to directly checking that the balance is at least 150 and the stock is greater than zero. The statement is literally the unfolding of the definition of `canPurchase`; it introduces no new mathematical content beyond the definition it references.

Since `Purchase.canPurchase` is defined (in Purchase.lean, lines 18-21) as the function `fun balance stock => 150 ≤ balance ∧ 0 < stock`, the right-hand side of the biconditional is literally the body of the definition. Thus the theorem is exactly the definitional unfolding of `canPurchase`: it asserts that a customer with `balance` dollars and `stock` units available is eligible to purchase precisely when the balance is at least 150 and the stock is positive. Concretely, reading the Nat inequalities numerically: the balance must be 150 or more, and the stock must be at least 1 (there is no upper bound on either quantity). This is a purely pointwise statement about a single predicate application; it says nothing about any transaction, state transition, or behaviour of a purchase operation, and it introduces no information beyond the definition it unfolds. The theorem carries no `sorry` and lists no non-standard axioms among its dependencies (only `Nat`, `Iff`, the `LE`/`LT` instances and `OfNat.ofNat` for the literal 150), so its proof is a definitional equality (`rfl`/`Iff.rfl`) rather than a substantive mathematical argument.

The only external items involved are the `LE`/`LT` instances on `Nat` and the literal `150` via `OfNat.ofNat`; no library semantics beyond standard natural-number comparison are required, and the meaning of `canPurchase` is fully available from the local definition.

Substituting the definition of `canPurchase`, this is the tautology `150 ≤ balance ∧ 0 < stock ↔ 150 ≤ balance ∧ 0 < stock`, i.e. a reflexive restatement of the definition's body with no new content.
